policy: Review every closed candidate set. Select only when ASV wording or an explicit mapped textual note distinguishes a reading; otherwise mark underdetermined and retain the base fallback. The base candidate is the SBLGNT reading.

decisions.evidence: ASV 'Are these things so?' renders the interrogative Ei alone; the added ara is an untranslated particle of inference that leaves no trace in English, so the ASV does not distinguish the readings.

ASV 'out of thy land, and from thy kindred' repeats the preposition in English, but ASV style repeats prepositions freely over a shared Greek one, so the repeated 'from' does not show a second ek stood in the text.
A bare Greek article before the noun has no separate English exponent here; 'thy kindred' reads the same with or without ten.
ASV 'And God spake on this wise' renders no dative addressee; the ASV renders a dative pronoun with a verb of speaking as 'unto him', and none appears, so the reading with auto is excluded.
ean and an are the same particle with the relative clause; 'the nation to which they shall be in bondage' renders either without distinction.
Future indicative and aorist subjunctive in this relative clause both come into English as 'they shall be in bondage'; the ASV wording does not separate them.
Word order only: 'said God' translates ho theos eipen and eipen ho theos alike, and English word order here is the translator's.
An article before the proper name has no English exponent; 'Abraham begat Isaac' is unchanged by ho.
An article before the proper name has no English exponent; 'Isaac begat Jacob' is unchanged by ho.
ASV 'governor over Egypt and all his house' carries one 'over' across both objects, which is idiomatic English whether or not a second eph' stood before holon ton oikon.
ASV reads 'a famine over all Egypt and Canaan' with no 'the land of'; the ASV renders ge as 'land' when it is present, so gen Aigyptou is excluded and the bare Aigypton stands.
ASV 'that there was grain in Egypt' renders either sitia eis Aigypton (eis in its stative sense) or sita en Aigypto; the form difference of the noun for grain is invisible in English.
ASV 'was made known to his brethren' translates the simple and the compounded passive identically; the ana- prefix leaves no English trace.
An article before genos has no separate English exponent; 'Joseph's race became manifest' reads the same either way.
Word order only: 'Jacob his father' renders both sequences, and the English order follows English idiom rather than the Greek.
ASV opens 'And Jacob went down', and the ASV renders both kai and a postpositive de as sentence-initial 'And'; the connective does not distinguish the readings.
ASV 'the tomb that Abraham bought' supplies one relative for either the dative ho (attracted to mnemati) or the accusative ho; English 'that' does not show the case.
ASV 'of the sons of Hamor in Shechem' renders en Sychem as a place; the RP tou Sychem would give the genealogical 'Hamor the father of Shechem', which the ASV does not print.
ASV 'which God vouchsafed unto Abraham' renders homologesen (promised, granted); omosen would require 'which God sware to Abraham', an oath the ASV does not print.
ASV 'another king over Egypt' renders ep' Aigypton; the RP reading omits the phrase and would leave 'there arose another king' with no 'over Egypt'.

ASV 'ill-treated our fathers' can render the articular tous pateras alone, since the ASV freely renders the article with a possessive when a speaker includes himself; the added hemon is not required by the English.
Word order only: 'cast out their babes' renders either sequence of ta brephe and ektheta.

Genitive absolute with a resumptive auton and the accusative participle construction both yield ASV 'and when he was cast out, Pharaoh's daughter took him up'; the syntactic difference is not visible in the English.

ASV 'was instructed in all the wisdom' renders a plain dative of sphere as readily as en with the dative, and the bracketed spelling of the name is orthographic; nothing in the English separates the three.
ASV 'mighty in his words and works' prints a possessive that has no source if autou is omitted; 'in words and works' would be idiomatic English for the RP reading, so the ASV's 'his' renders autou.
ASV 'that his brethren understood' can render the articular tous adelphous, where English requires a possessive for the article; the explicit autou is not shown by the wording.
Word order only: 'was giving them deliverance' renders either sequence of soterian and autois.
ASV 'would have set them at one again' renders synellassen, to reconcile; synelasen (drove them together, urged them) would not give a reconciling sense, and the ASV prints no such wording.
ASV 'ye are brethren' carries the subject in the verb; an added emphatic hymeis would not be separately rendered.
eph' hemon and eph' hemas both come into English as 'over us'; the case difference has no exponent in the ASV.
echthes and chthes are spellings of the same adverb; 'yesterday' renders both.
ASV 'an angel appeared to him' has no 'of the Lord'; the RP angelos kyriou would require 'an angel of the Lord', which the ASV does not print.
ASV 'he wondered at the sight' renders aorist and imperfect alike; the ASV does not mark the aspectual difference here.
ASV ends the verse at 'there came a voice of the Lord,' with no 'unto him'; pros auton would be rendered and is absent.
ASV 'the God of Abraham, and of Isaac' does not repeat 'the God' before Isaac; the RP addition of ho theos would require the repeated noun.
ASV 'and of Isaac, and of Jacob' does not repeat 'the God' before Jacob either; the RP addition of ho theos would require the repeated noun.
ASV 'the place whereon thou standest' renders eph' and en alike; the preposition is absorbed in 'whereon'.
ASV 'heard their groaning' follows 'my people', a collective the ASV can resume with a plural possessive; autou (of the people) and auton are both compatible with 'their'.
Hortatory aorist subjunctive and future indicative both come into English as 'I will send thee'; the ASV does not distinguish them.
ASV 'to be both a ruler and a deliverer' renders the correlative kai ... kai; without the first kai the ASV would print 'a ruler and a deliverer' with no 'both'.
ASV 'him hath God sent' renders the perfect apestalken; the RP aorist apesteilen would give 'God sent'. The prepositions syn and en would both yield 'with the hand', so the tense is what decides.
ASV 'wonders and signs in Egypt' prints no 'land'; the ASV renders ge as 'land' where it stands, so en ge Aigypto is excluded and the articular en te Aigypto stands.
eipas and eipon are alternative aorist participles of the same verb; 'who said' renders both.
ASV 'A prophet shall God raise up unto you' names God alone; the RP kyrios ho theos hemon would require 'the Lord our God', which the ASV does not print.
ASV 'who received living oracles' is plural, rendering logia zonta; the RP singular logon would give 'a living word'.
ASV 'to give unto us' renders hemin; the WH hymin would require 'unto you'.
ASV 'turned back in their hearts unto Egypt' is plural, rendering en tais kardiais; the RP singular te kardia would give 'in their heart'.

ASV 'we know not what is become of him' renders the aorist egeneto in this indirect question as readily as the perfect gegonen; the English perfect here is idiomatic rather than a marker of the Greek tense.
ASV 'the star of the god Rephan' has no possessive; the added hymon would require 'your god'.

ASV prints 'Rephan', which excludes the WH Rompha and the RP Remphan with its intrusive mu (the KJV's 'Remphan'); Rhaiphan and Rhephan both transliterate to 'Rephan' in ASV practice, so the English does not choose between them.
ASV 'a habitation for the God of Jacob' renders to theo Iakob; the NA oiko would require 'for the house of Jacob'.
ASV 'dwelleth not in houses made with hands' supplies the general noun 'houses' to cheiropoietois; the RP naois would give 'temples made with hands', which the ASV does not print.
ASV 'And the earth the footstool of my feet' renders a connective the ASV writes as 'And' whether the Greek reads he de or kai he.
ASV 'uncircumcised in heart and ears' uses the fixed Hebraic idiom, in which the singular 'heart' stands for the plural kardiais as readily as for te kardia; the English number is not decisive.
ASV 'of whom ye have now become betrayers' renders the aorist egenesthe with nyn as naturally as the perfect gegenesthe; the English perfect does not settle the Greek tense.
dienoigmenous and aneogmenous are synonymous perfect passive participles; 'the heavens opened' renders both.
ASV 'laid down their garments' requires a possessive in English whatever the Greek reads, so 'their' does not show that auton stood in the text.
Word order only: 'lay not this sin to their charge' renders either sequence of tauten and ten hamartian.
